claims: If gross income from an activity consisting in major part of breeding, training, showing, or racing of horses exceeds deductions attributable to such activity in 2 of 7 consecutive taxable years, the activity is presumed to be engaged in for profit unless the Commissioner establishes to the contrary

If claim 1 is true, sources confirm this meets the section 183(d) presumption criteria for horse activities.

claims: The home office deduction requires that the space be used exclusively and regularly for business purposes

claims: A home office deduction can create a loss if the expenses exceed the income earned from the business
No deduction is allowed for a home office unless it is used exclusively on a regular basis as the taxpayer's principal place of business

claims: To deduct business gifts, a taxpayer must substantiate the cost and description of the gift
To deduct business gifts, a taxpayer must substantiate the date the gift was made
To deduct business gifts, a taxpayer must substantiate the business reason for the gift

Section 274(d) requires adequate records or sufficient evidence corroborating the amount.
Section 274(d) requires adequate records or sufficient evidence corroborating time and place.
Section 274(d) requires adequate records or sufficient evidence corroborating business purpose.
Section 274(d) requires adequate records or sufficient evidence corroborating business relationship.

claims: Only 50 percent of meal expenses is allowed as a deduction under U.S. tax law

claims: A business can deduct no more than $25 for gifts given directly or indirectly to a single recipient during the taxable year

claims: Travel expenses incurred by a self-employed individual while away from home in pursuit of a trade or business may be deductible under section 162(a)(2).

claims: The aggregate cost of section 179 property that a taxpayer may elect to expense under section 179 for any taxable year is subject to a dollar limitation

claims: If the business use of a car falls to 50% or less, the taxpayer can no longer use an accelerated depreciation method for that car

claims: To qualify as a real estate professional for the tax year, you must perform more than 750 hours of services during the tax year in real property trades or businesses in which you materially participate

verdicts.why: 26 U.S.C. § 469(c)(7)(B)(ii) states this requirement is necessary to qualify as a real estate professional.

claims: A taxpayer who actively participates in a rental real estate activity may deduct a maximum loss of $25,000 per year related to the activity

claims: Self-employment income does not include net earnings from self-employment when the amount of such earnings for the taxable year is less than $400

claims: For purposes of determining a substantial understatement of income tax for an individual, the understatement must exceed the greater of 10 percent of the tax required to be shown on the return or $5,000

verdicts.why: 26 U.S.C. § 6662(d)(1)(A) states substantial understatement occurs when understatement exceeds greater of 10% of required tax or $5,000 for individuals.

claims: The accuracy-related penalty on an underpayment is equal to 20% of the underpayment

verdicts.why: 26 U.S.C. § 6662(a) states the accuracy-related penalty equals 20% of the underpayment to which the section applies.

claims: A taxpayer may avoid a section 6662(a) penalty by showing that there was reasonable cause for the underpayment and that the taxpayer acted in good faith
The determination of whether a taxpayer acted with reasonable cause and in good faith is made on a case-by-case basis

claims: Under Internal Revenue Code section 7491, the burden of proof shifts to the IRS when the taxpayer introduces credible evidence with respect to a factual issue relevant to ascertaining the taxpayer's tax liability
To shift the burden of proof to the IRS, the taxpayer must comply with all applicable substantiation requirements
To shift the burden of proof to the IRS, the taxpayer must maintain all required records
To shift the burden of proof to the IRS, the taxpayer must cooperate with reasonable requests for information from the IRS regarding the factual issue

claims: If a taxpayer omits more than 25 percent of gross income from their tax return, the IRS may assess tax or begin collection proceedings at any time within six years after the return was filed
For determining gross income, total amounts received or accrued from the sale of goods or services must be considered without deducting costs

claims: The IRS normally has 3 years to assess additional tax after a client files their return

claims: A claim for credit or refund of an overpayment of tax must be filed within 3 years from the time the return was filed or 2 years from the time the tax was paid, whichever period expires later

claims: A corporation or partnership meets the gross receipts test if its average annual gross receipts for the 3-taxable-year period does not exceed $25,000,000

claims: For self-employment income tax purposes, the term 'employee' has the same meaning as under the Federal Insurance Contributions Act (FICA)

claims: Groceries and household bills are generally considered personal expenses and are not deductible as business costs

claims: Internal Revenue Code Section 280E disallows deductions or credits for any amount paid or incurred in carrying on the trade or business of trafficking in controlled substances

claims: Under the cash method of accounting, you must include in your gross income all items of income you actually or constructively receive during your tax year

claims: The Tax Court held that CRP payments are includible in self-employment income under I.R.C. sec. 1401 because the taxpayer was engaged in a trade or business during the years in issue and there was a nexus between the trade or business and the CRP payments received

claims: A taxpayer may qualify for section 530 relief from employment taxes if it did not treat an individual as an employee for any period

claims: The sole shareholder and president of an S corporation is considered an employee for employment tax purposes under section 3121(d)(1)

claims: If an IRA custodian's check is routed through the IRA owner to buy stock for the IRA, it does not constitute a taxable distribution to the owner if the owner does not have unfettered control over the funds

claims: Taxpayers may not deduct expenses for a bed and breakfast if they used the bed and breakfast for personal purposes for an indeterminate period and failed to substantiate the expenses

claims: A taxpayer cannot deduct a loss for money forfeited to the government after a criminal conviction

claims: Section 280E provides that no deduction is allowed for amounts paid in carrying on any trade or business if such business consists of trafficking in controlled substances which is prohibited by state or federal law

Sources state section 280E addresses deductions and credits, not reasonable collection potential computation.

claims: A penalty approval form that only refers to individual partners does not satisfy the written supervisory approval requirement for penalties against the partnership

claims: Vehicles used only to drive passengers for hire are not subject to the strict substantiation requirements of section 274(d)

claims: The expenses of bowling activities are deductible only if the taxpayer has a profit motive for those activities

claims: The Tax Court allows a home office deduction if the space is used exclusively and regularly as the principal place of business for any trade or business of the taxpayer

claims: No deduction is allowed for an activity not engaged in for profit under section 183(a)

claims: Settlement money paid into a lawyer's trust account is generally considered income to the taxpayer when it is paid into the account, not when it is released

claims: A taxpayer qualifies as a real estate professional if more than one-half of their personal services are performed in real property trades or businesses in which they materially participate

claims: The 90-day filing deadline in I.R.C. § 6234(a) is not jurisdictional

claims: The sole shareholder and president of an S corporation is considered an employee for employment tax purposes under section 3121(d)(1)
A corporation cannot claim section 530 relief if it had no reasonable basis for not treating the shareholder as an employee
Section 530 relief is limited to worker classification issues arising under common law
Statutory employees are not eligible for section 530 relief

verdicts.why: 119 T.C. No. 5 holds that an officer and sole shareholder of an S corporation is an employee within the meaning of sections 3121(d)(1) and 3306(i) for employment tax purposes.
119 T.C. No. 5 holds that section 530 relief requires reasonable basis and the corporation had none, thus is not entitled to relief.
119 T.C. No. 5 holds that section 530 is limited to controversies involving employment tax status under common law, excluding statutory employees.
119 T.C. No. 5 questions whether section 530 ever applies to statutory employees and concludes it is limited to common law classification issues.

claims: If an IRA custodian's check is routed through the IRA owner to buy stock for the IRA, it is not considered a taxable distribution to the owner if the owner does not have unfettered control over the funds
A distribution occurs when the IRA owner has actual and unfettered possession of the IRA assets, which allows them to exercise complete dominion over it
When a check issued by the custodian to the IRA owner is then forwarded to purchase stock for the IRA, it does not constitute a distribution if the IRA owner is acting as a conduit for the custodian

verdicts.why: Ancira case holds no distribution when owner acts as conduit lacking unfettered control; stock issued in IRA's name.
Sources state taxable income occurs when taxpayer has complete dominion and unfettered command over funds.
Ancira explicitly holds petitioner was conduit for custodian; no distribution resulted from check routing through owner.

claims: The acquisition by an individual retirement account of any collectible is treated as a distribution from such account in an amount equal to the cost to such account of such collectible
American Eagle coins are considered collectibles under the Internal Revenue Code
An owner of a self-directed IRA may not take actual and unfettered possession of the IRA assets, as this constitutes a taxable distribution
When coins or bullion are in the physical possession of the IRA owner, there is no independent oversight that could prevent the owner from invading retirement funds

verdicts.why: 26 U.S.C. § 408(m)(1) states acquisition of any collectible by an IRA is treated as a distribution equal to the cost.
Sources show American Eagle coins are excepted from collectible definition under 26 U.S.C. § 408(m)(3) when held by trustee.
Tax Court held in McNulty case that IRA owner taking actual unfettered possession of IRA assets constitutes taxable distribution.
Tax Court opinion states lack of independent oversight when owner has physical possession is inconsistent with statutory scheme.

claims: The contribution of cash instead of a partnership interest does not qualify as a rollover contribution under section 408(d)(3)(A)(i)
Section 408(d)(3)(A)(i) requires that the same property be transferred in a rollover, not merely similar property or property of equivalent value
Changing the character of property from a partnership interest to cash violates the rollover rules
A taxpayer is limited to one nontaxable rollover of an IRA distribution per one-year period

verdicts.why: Tax Court held that liquidating partnership interest and contributing cash proceeds does not qualify as rollover under 408(d)(3)(A)(i).
Sources state section 408(d)(3)(A)(i) requires 'the same property' be transferred, not merely similar or equivalent value property.
Tax Court explicitly held changing noncash property character from partnership interest to cash violates rollover requirements.
IRC 408(d)(3)(B) limits taxpayers to one nontaxable rollover of IRA distribution per one-year period.

claims: A rental activity is generally treated as a passive activity regardless of whether the taxpayer materially participates in that activity
If a taxpayer qualifies as a real estate professional and meets material participation requirements, the rental activity may not be classified as passive
To qualify as a real estate professional, the taxpayer must perform more than one-half of their personal services in real property trades or businesses in which they materially participate
To qualify as a real estate professional, the taxpayer must perform more than 750 hours of services during the taxable year in real property trades or businesses
If a taxpayer meets the real estate professional criteria, lease income from the property may be treated as non-passive income

verdicts.why: Multiple sources state rental activities are per se passive regardless of material participation.
Sources indicate real estate professionals are not subject to per se passive activity classification if material participation requirements are met.
26 U.S.C. § 469(c)(7)(B) explicitly requires more than one-half of personal services in real property trades or businesses where taxpayer materially participates.
26 U.S.C. § 469(c)(7)(B) explicitly requires more than 750 hours of services in real property trades or businesses where taxpayer materially participates.
26 CFR 1.469-2(f)(6) treats gross rental income as not from passive activity for property rented to trade or business where taxpayer materially participates.

claims: The codified economic substance doctrine requires a relevancy determination before it can be applied to a transaction
Section 7701(o)(1) states that the economic substance doctrine applies only to transactions to which it is relevant
The determination of whether the economic substance doctrine is relevant to a transaction must be made in the same manner as if section 7701(o) had never been enacted

verdicts.why: Court held section 7701(o) requires a relevancy determination before applying the doctrine.
Section 7701(o)(1) text states doctrine applies to transactions to which it is relevant.
Section 7701(o)(5)(C) expressly requires determination made as if subsection had never been enacted.

claims: The 90-day deadline in section 6234(a) is subject to equitable tolling
For equitable tolling to apply, the petitioner must establish that they pursued their rights diligently
For equitable tolling to apply, extraordinary circumstances outside of the petitioner's control must have prevented them from filing on time
The burden is on the petitioner to demonstrate that equitable tolling applies to their specific circumstances

verdicts.why: Tax Court held that nothing in section 6234(a) rebuts the presumption favoring equitable tolling; the 90-day deadline is subject to equitable tolling.
Tax Court held that for equitable tolling to apply, petitioner must establish (1) it pursued its rights diligently and (2) extraordinary circumstances prevented timely filing.
Tax Court held for equitable tolling to apply, extraordinary circumstances outside petitioner's control must have prevented filing on time.
Tax Court held the burden is on the petitioner to establish that equitable tolling applies to their specific circumstances.

claims: Section 274(d) strict substantiation requirements generally apply to pickup trucks and vans unless the truck or van has been specially modified so it is not likely to be used more than a de minimis amount for personal purposes
Section 274(d) excludes qualified nonpersonal use vehicles from strict substantiation requirements
Qualified nonpersonal use vehicles include vehicles that are not likely to be used more than a de minimis amount for personal purposes
Pickup trucks that have been modified for business use and are not likely to be used for personal purposes are not subject to strict substantiation requirements under section 274(d)
Examples of modifications that may qualify a pickup truck as a nonpersonal use vehicle include attachments for specific farming tasks such as transporting hay or livestock

verdicts.why: 26 CFR 1.274-5(k)(8) and court cases state this rule applies to pickup trucks and vans unless specially modified.
T.C. Memo. 2024-91 and other sources confirm section 274(d) excludes qualified nonpersonal use vehicles from strict substantiation requirements.
IRC § 274(i) defines qualified nonpersonal use vehicle as not likely to be used more than de minimis amount for personal purposes.
T.C. Memo. 2022-117 holds that specially modified pickup trucks not likely used for personal purposes are exempt from strict substantiation.
T.C. Memo. 2022-117 provides examples: hay-transporting truck with bale stabber and livestock transport trucks with attached trailers.

claims: The Cohan rule allows the Tax Court to estimate business expenses when a taxpayer establishes that an expense is deductible but cannot substantiate the precise amount
Under the Cohan rule, the taxpayer must present some credible evidence that provides a rational basis for the estimate
If the taxpayer fails to produce adequate records or proof of payment, the Tax Court may decline to estimate the expenses under the Cohan rule
The burden of substantiating expenses rests with the taxpayer
The Tax Court bears heavily against the taxpayer whose inexactitude is of their own making

verdicts.why: Multiple sources state Cohan allows estimation when taxpayer establishes deductible expense but cannot substantiate precise amount.
Sources explicitly state taxpayer must present credible evidence providing rational basis for estimate under Cohan.
Sources indicate Court may decline Cohan estimation where proper recordkeeping feasible and expected, or insufficient evidence.
Multiple sources state burden of substantiating expenses rests with taxpayer.
Sources directly state Court bears heavily against taxpayer whose inexactitude is of their own making.

claims: A taxpayer is treated as materially participating in an activity if they materially participated in the activity for any five out of the ten years immediately preceding the taxable year
The five of ten test applies to an activity that is the same over time
Regulations allow for a comparison of current-year activities with preceding-year activities if there are changes

If there is substantial similarity between the current-year activity and activities that the taxpayer materially participated in during a preceding year, then that preceding year counts as one year in applying the five of ten test to the current-year activity

A taxpayer is treated as materially participating in an activity for a prior taxable year if the activity includes significant section 469 activities that are substantially the same as those in which the taxpayer materially participated during that prior taxable year

verdicts.why: 26 CFR 1.469-5T(a)(5) and T.C. Memo 2022-49 directly state this rule.
T.C. Memo 2022-49 at *15 explicitly states 'By its terms, the five of ten test applies to an activity that is the same over time.'
T.C. Memo 2022-49 at *15-16 explains regulations allow comparison when activities change.
T.C. Memo 2022-49 at *16 explicitly confirms preceding year counts if substantial similarity exists.
26 CFR 1.469-5(j)(1) and T.C. Memo 2022-49 state this rule using 'significant section 469 activities.'

claims: A taxpayer qualifies as a real estate professional under Section 469 if more than one-half of the personal services performed in trades and businesses by the taxpayer during the taxable year are performed in real property trades or businesses in which the taxpayer materially participates

A taxpayer qualifies as a real estate professional under Section 469 if the taxpayer performs more than 750 hours of services during the taxable year in real property trades or businesses in which the taxpayer materially participates

If a taxpayer has a full-time job and cannot show that they spent more time in real estate than in their other work, they will not meet the requirement that more than one-half of their personal services are in real property trades or businesses
A taxpayer with a full-time job who does not meet the more-than-one-half personal services requirement would not qualify as a real estate professional for the taxable year

verdicts.why: 26 U.S.C. § 469(c)(7)(B)(i) states this requirement explicitly.
26 U.S.C. § 469(c)(7)(B)(ii) states this requirement explicitly.
T.C. Memo. 2022-112 case held taxpayers with full-time jobs who couldn't show more time in real estate don't meet the one-half requirement.
§ 469(c)(7)(B) requires both conditions; failing one means real estate professional status is not achieved.

claims: Taxpayers may not deduct expenses for a bed and breakfast if they used the property for personal purposes for an indeterminate period
Taxpayers must substantiate expenses to claim deductions related to a bed and breakfast operation

verdicts.why: Tax Court held petitioners cannot deduct B&B expenses because they used it for personal purposes for indeterminate period.
Tax Court cited failed substantiation of expenses as additional reason to deny B&B deductions.

claims: A taxpayer cannot deduct a loss for money forfeited to the government after a criminal conviction
Forfeitures are considered penalties that frustrate public policy
Losses arising from illegal activities, including criminal forfeitures, are not deductible under section 165
Forfeited funds are treated as gross income to the taxpayer
Forfeited funds are considered realized benefits

verdicts.why: Sources establish that section 165 loss deductions are disallowed for criminal forfeitures on public policy grounds.
T.C. Memo 2025-32 states criminal forfeitures are 'penalties' that the Tank Truck Rentals doctrine prohibits deducting to preserve penalty 'sting'.
T.C. Memo 2024-16 and 2025-32 confirm losses from illegal activities and criminal forfeitures are not deductible under section 165.
T.C. Memo 2024-16 states forfeited funds must be recognized as gross income; taxpayers constructively receive them.
T.C. Memo 2024-16 explicitly states by forfeiting funds, the taxpayer 'has realized the benefits of them.'

claims: Section 280E provides that no deduction is allowed for amounts paid in carrying on any trade or business if such business consists of trafficking in controlled substances which is prohibited by state or federal law
The IRS has an established policy to disregard business expenses that are rendered nondeductible by section 280E when evaluating an offer in compromise from a cannabis business
Rejecting an offer in compromise solely on the basis of an understanding that section 280E required the disallowance of business expenses would be an error
Section 280E addresses deductions and credits, not the computation of reasonable collection potential

verdicts.why: Source explicitly states section 280E disallows deductions for trafficking in controlled substances prohibited by state or federal law.
Source confirms Commissioner has established policy to disregard section 280E nondeductible expenses in offer-in-compromise evaluation.
Source states rejecting offer solely on basis that section 280E required disallowance would be an error.
Source explicitly states section 280E addresses deductions and credits, not reasonable collection potential computation.

claims: A penalty approval form that only refers to individual partners does not satisfy the written supervisory approval requirement for penalties against the partnership
The written supervisory approval requirement mandates that the approval must reflect the supervisor's intent to approve the penalty against the partnership, not just individual partners
If a penalty approval form identifies individual partners rather than the partnership itself, it fails to meet the written supervisory approval requirement

verdicts.why: T.C. Memo. 2022-52 at *37-39 holds that a Civil Penalty Approval Form identifying only individual partners does not satisfy section 6751(b)(1) for partnership-level penalties.
T.C. Memo. 2022-52 at *37 states the form must manifest the supervisor's intent to approve penalties against the partnership, not just individuals.
T.C. Memo. 2022-52 at *37 explicitly holds that a form identifying individual partners rather than the partnership fails to satisfy written supervisory approval requirement.

claims: Vehicles used to drive passengers for hire are not subject to the strict substantiation requirements of section 274(d)
The term qualified nonpersonal use vehicle includes vehicles used directly in the trade or business of transporting persons for compensation or hire

verdicts.why: 26 CFR 1.280F-6(c)(3)(ii) excludes vehicles used in transporting persons for compensation or hire from passenger automobile definition, and 26 CFR 1.274-5(k)(1) exempts qualified nonpersonal use vehicles from section 274(d) substantiation.
26 CFR 1.280F-6(c)(3)(ii) states passenger automobiles do not include vehicles used directly in transporting persons for compensation or hire, supporting qualified nonpersonal use vehicle status.

claims: The Tax Court has ruled that expenses related to bowling activities are only deductible if the taxpayer has a profit motive for those activities
If bowling activities are not engaged in for profit, then no deductions are allowable for the expenses of the activity under Section 183(a)
In the case of Bruce E. Phillips, the Tax Court found that he did not have a profit motive for his bowling activities
Bruce E. Phillips's bowling expenses were not deductible

verdicts.why: Sources state bowling expenses are deductible only if profit motive exists per Section 183(a)
Section 183(a) explicitly stated in sources: no deductions allowed if activity not engaged in for profit
Court concluded Mr. Phillips did not engage in bowling activities for profit based on facts and circumstances
Court held no deductions allowed because Phillips lacked profit motive and failed substantiation requirements

claims: The Tax Court allows a home office deduction if the space is used exclusively and regularly as the principal place of business for any trade or business of the taxpayer
A taxpayer must prove that the claimed portion of the home was used exclusively for business purposes to qualify for the deduction
Exclusive use is an all-or-nothing standard, meaning that if the space is used for both personal and business purposes, the deduction will not be allowed
If an in-law suite is converted and used exclusively for business, it may qualify for the home office deduction
A taxpayer must demonstrate that a spare room was used exclusively for work and not for any personal use to qualify for the home office deduction

verdicts.why: 26 U.S.C. § 280A(c)(1)(A) and Tax Court cases establish this standard for home office deductions.
Multiple Tax Court cases require taxpayers prove exclusive use for business as principal place of business.
Hamacher v. Commissioner establishes exclusive use is an all-or-nothing standard; cases deny deductions for mixed personal-business use.
T.C. Memo. 2013-80 allowed deduction for converted in-law suite with separate entrance used exclusively for business.
Tax Court cases consistently deny deductions for spare rooms without proof of exclusive business use and principal place of business status.

claims: No deduction is allowed for an activity not engaged in for profit under section 183(a)
An activity is not engaged in for profit if it does not meet the requirements of section 162 or section 212
If an activity is determined to be not engaged in for profit, then deductions attributable to that activity are limited to the gross income derived from it under section 183(b)
Home office deductions are subject to the exclusive use requirement under section 280A(c)(1)
If the activity is not engaged in for profit, then the home office expenses related to that activity are not deductible

verdicts.why: 26 U.S.C. § 183(a) states no deduction is allowed except as provided in the section.
26 CFR 1.183-2(a) defines 'activity not engaged in for profit' as any activity other than one allowable under section 162 or 212.
26 U.S.C. § 183(b) limits deductions to gross income from the activity for activities not engaged in for profit.
T.C. Memo. 2023-128 states home office deductions require exclusive use under section 280A(c)(1).
T.C. Memo. 2023-128 holds that if activity lacks profit motive, it fails the section 280A(c)(1) trade or business requirement, making home office expenses non-deductible.

claims: The Tax Court found that spa workers who pay booth rent can be classified as independent contractors rather than employees

In Cheryl A. Mayfield Therapy Center v. Commissioner, the court concluded that service providers were independent contractors based on factors including their autonomy and the nature of their payment arrangement
Service providers who paid fixed booth rent and retained the right to control their work schedules and client interactions were classified as independent contractors
The lack of employee benefits provided to service providers is a factor favoring independent contractor status
Service providers' significant investments in their own business operations is a factor favoring independent contractor status

verdicts.why: Tax Court held in T.C. Memo. 2010-239 that spa service providers paying booth rent were independent contractors, not employees.
Court concluded service providers were independent contractors based on autonomy factors and payment arrangement including booth rent.
Sources show fixed booth rent, control over schedules and client refusal rights supported independent contractor classification.
Sources explicitly state lack of employee benefits supports independent contractor status in the analysis.
Sources note massage therapists' significant investments in decorating rooms counted as factor favoring independent contractor status.

claims: Settlement money paid into a lawyer's trust account is generally considered income to the taxpayer in the year it is paid into the account, not when it is released
The constructive receipt doctrine does not apply if the taxpayer did not delay the payment of the settlement amount
In the case of funds deposited into a trust account pending resolution of a fee dispute, the taxpayer is considered to have received the income at the time of the deposit

verdicts.why: Gale and Young cases establish settlement money in trust account is income when paid to attorney, not when released.
T.C. Memo. 2002-54 explicitly states constructive receipt doctrine need not be considered if taxpayer did not delay payment.
Gale case holds funds paid to attorney's trust account pending fee dispute resolution are taxable income at time of deposit.

claims: Under Internal Revenue Code Section 183, a taxpayer generally may not deduct expenses incurred in connection with a hobby or other non-profit activity to offset taxable income from other sources
The client's activity of restoring and selling vintage bikes is considered a hobby under Section 183 because it is unprofitable
The client cannot deduct the $5,000 in expenses against the $3,000 earned from the hobby

verdicts.why: T.C. Memo. 2009-220 states that a taxpayer generally may not deduct expenses incurred in connection with a hobby or other non-profit activity to offset taxable income from other sources under Section 183(a).
Unprofitability alone does not determine hobby status. T.C. Memo. 2009-220 and 2023-5 show profit motive requires analyzing multiple factors beyond just losses.
Whether deductions are allowed depends on whether the activity is a hobby under Section 183, which requires fact-intensive analysis not determinable from provided sources.

claims: Conservation Reserve Program payments received by a taxpayer are includible in self-employment income under IRC section 1401 if the taxpayer is engaged in a trade or business during the years in issue and there is a nexus between the trade or business and the CRP payments received
Conservation Reserve Program payments do not constitute rentals from real estate within the meaning of IRC section 1402(a)(1)
Conservation Reserve Program payments are not excluded from the calculation of net earnings from self-employment
A taxpayer may conduct their trade or business personally or through an agent
Activities performed by an agent can result in self-employment tax liability for the taxpayer
A nexus between a trade or business and CRP payments received is necessary for self-employment tax applicability to those CRP payments

verdicts.why: Case held CRP payments includible in self-employment income when engaged in trade or business with nexus to CRP payments.
Court held CRP payments do not constitute 'rentals from real estate' under IRC 1402(a)(1).
Court held CRP payments not excluded from net earnings calculation under section 1402(a)(1).
Sources state taxpayer may conduct trade or business personally or through agents under regulations.
Sources state agent's activities performing contractual obligations create taxpayer's self-employment tax liability.
Court held CRP payments includible when nexus existed between trade or business and payments.

claims: A taxpayer qualifies as a real estate professional if more than one-half of their personal services are performed in real property trades or businesses in which they materially participate
A real estate professional must perform more than 750 hours of services during the taxable year in real property trades or businesses
When a taxpayer qualifies as a real estate professional, rental activities are not per se passive activities under section 469(c)(2)
A real estate professional must still meet the material participation requirement for each individual rental activity to treat losses from that activity as nonpassive
When a taxpayer has not elected to treat multiple rental houses as a single activity, each house is treated as a separate activity for determining material participation
The client is heavily involved in only two of the six rental houses
Losses from rental activities in which a taxpayer is not heavily involved may be considered passive unless the taxpayer meets the material participation requirement for those properties

verdicts.why: 26 U.S.C. § 469(c)(7)(B)(i) requires more than one-half of personal services in real property trades or businesses in which taxpayer materially participates.
26 U.S.C. § 469(c)(7)(B)(ii) requires more than 750 hours of services in real property trades or businesses in which taxpayer materially participates.
T.C. Memo. 2010-232 states rental activities of real estate professionals are 'not per se passive activities under section 469(c)(2)'.
T.C. Memo. 2010-232 and sources confirm real estate professionals remain subject to material participation requirement of section 469(c)(1).
26 U.S.C. § 469(c)(7)(A)(ii) provides each interest in rental real estate is treated as separate activity absent election.
Sources do not provide information about client's actual involvement level in the six houses.
26 CFR 1.469-9(e) example shows losses from properties without material participation remain passive despite real estate professional status.

claims: An S corporation can deduct rent payments made to shareholders for board meetings held at their homes if the payments are reasonable and substantiated
Under the 14-day rule, rental income from the rental of a taxpayer's residence is not included in gross income if the residence is rented for no more than 14 days in a taxable year
If an S corporation's rent payments are deemed excessive or not substantiated, the IRS may disallow the deductions

verdicts.why: Sources show courts disallow such deductions even when payments are substantiated, finding them tax avoidance schemes.
26 U.S.C. § 280A(g) and case law confirm rental income excluded if residence rented ≤14 days annually.
T.C. Memo. 2023-105 demonstrates IRS disallowed rent deductions for lack of substantiation and unreasonableness.

claims: The presumption that an activity is engaged in for profit arises if gross income exceeds deductions for any 2 of 5 consecutive taxable years, unless the Commissioner establishes otherwise
The presumption does not apply when a client has only one profitable year in eight years
The Tax Court considers the existence of a business plan when determining profit motive
The Tax Court considers changes in operating methods to improve profitability when determining profit motive
The Tax Court considers the amount of occasional profits when determining profit motive
A long period of losses without serious consideration of discontinuing an activity may indicate a lack of profit motive
The Tax Court may conclude that a taxpayer did not engage in an activity with the requisite profit objective if there are significant losses and personal motives are present

verdicts.why: 26 CFR 1.183-1(c)(1) states presumption arises if gross income exceeds deductions for 2 of 5 consecutive years for horse activities, unless Commissioner establishes otherwise.
One profitable year in eight years fails the 2-of-5 or 2-of-7 year test, so presumption does not arise under 26 CFR 1.183-1(c)(1).
T.C. Memo. 2012-17 states businesslike operation characteristics include preparation of business plan, cited in horse breeding cases.
26 CFR 1.183-2(b)(1) and T.C. Memo. 2012-17 indicate profit motive shown when taxpayer changes operating methods to improve profitability.
T.C. Memo. 2013-54 states amount of occasional profits is factor showing profit motive under 26 CFR 1.183-2(b)(7).
T.C. Memo. 2013-294 finds lack of profit motive where taxpayer continued 17 years without approaching profitability without seriously considering discontinuing.
T.C. Memo. 2013-294 concludes no requisite profit objective where significant losses and personal motives present after weighing all facts.

claims: An officer of a corporation is generally considered an employee of that corporation for employment tax purposes under 26 U.S.C. § 3121(d)(1)

An officer who does not perform any services or performs only minor services and does not receive any remuneration is not considered an employee of the corporation for employment tax purposes under 26 U.S.C. § 3121(d)

An officer who is the only officer and only person working for the corporation and takes no salary may not be considered an employee for employment tax purposes if the officer performs only minor services and does not receive remuneration

verdicts.why: 26 U.S.C. § 3121(d)(1) states officers of corporations are employees; 119 T.C. No. 5 confirms officers are generally employees.
119 T.C. No. 5 cites regulation limiting § 3121(d)(1): officer performing no/minor services and receiving no remuneration is not an employee.
Directly follows from Claim 1: regulation excludes officers from employee status if performing only minor services and receiving no remuneration.

claims: The common law test for determining independent contractor status considers the degree of control exercised by the employer, the permanency of the relationship, and whether the services provided are integral to the employer's business
If workers perform services that are an essential part of the employer's business, this supports an employer-employee relationship, regardless of the duration of their employment
If a worker does not work regularly but works in the course of the employer's trade or business, this may indicate an employee relationship
The degree of control, the right to discharge, and the integral nature of work supported a finding that certain drivers were employees rather than independent contractors
The relationship the parties believed they were creating, such as issuing Forms 1099 instead of W-2s, does not override the actual nature of the relationship as determined by the facts

verdicts.why: Sources discuss control, permanency of relationship, and whether services are integral to business as factors in the common law test.
T.C. Memo. 2000-375 states drivers performing essential services integral to business supports employee relationship, regardless of brief employment duration.
Both T.C. cases state that irregular work in course of employer's trade or business does not prevent employee classification.
T.C. Memo. 2000-375 explicitly states degree of control, right to discharge, and integral nature of work supported finding drivers were employees.
T.C. Memo. 2007-66 states that written contractor agreements and Forms 1099 are overridden by actual facts showing control and integration.

claims: Proceeds from a life insurance policy received from a nonqualified employee benefit trust are generally not includible in gross income under section 101 of the Internal Revenue Code
The policy had no cash surrender value after charges
The amount received from the life insurance policy would be the death benefit minus any cash surrender value
The amount taxable to the client from the life insurance proceeds is zero

verdicts.why: Sources address qualified plans and trusts under 401(a), not nonqualified employee benefit trusts.
This is a factual statement from the question itself.
Sources do not establish the formula for calculating taxable amount from life insurance policy distributions.
Sources do not provide sufficient information to determine the taxable amount for this nonqualified trust distribution scenario.

claims: The IRS allows a deduction for reasonable compensation paid to employees, including corporate officers, under section 162(a)(1)
Compensation that exceeds $1,000,000 is subject to limitations under 26 CFR 1.162-27(e)(2)
Compensation for a majority shareholder-officer must be evaluated against what would ordinarily be paid for similar services by similar enterprises under similar circumstances
If compensation is found to be excessive compared to industry standards, the excess may not be deductible as a business expense
Compensation that constitutes a disguised dividend is not deductible

verdicts.why: Sources discuss section 162(a)(1) allowing deductions for reasonable compensation paid to employees and corporate officers.
26 CFR 1.162-27(e)(2) addresses performance-based compensation requirements, not a blanket $1,000,000 limitation.
T.C. Memo 2004-207 cites regulation 1.162-7(b)(3) requiring compensation be 'ordinarily paid for like services by like enterprises under like circumstances.'
T.C. Memo 2004-207 disallowed excess compensation exceeding reasonable industry standards as non-deductible business expense.
T.C. Memo 2004-207 explicitly held compensation excess constituting disguised dividend is not deductible.

claims: Income from a rental activity is generally treated as passive activity income under section 469
If a taxpayer is involved in a self-rental situation, the income may be recharacterized as nonpassive income under the self-rental rule
In a self-rental situation, each item of property such as each tractor or trailer is treated separately for purposes of determining passive activity losses and income

A taxpayer must accept the tax consequences of how they structured their business transactions, which may prevent netting of income and losses from different entities if they are treated as separate items of property

verdicts.why: Section 469(c)(2) states rental activities are generally treated as passive activities.
Tax Court case and regulations discuss self-rental rule recharacterization under section 1.469-2(f)(6).
139 T.C. No. 3 holds each tractor and trailer is separate item of property under self-rental rule.
139 T.C. No. 3 states taxpayers must accept tax consequences of their business structure choices.

claims: Amounts paid for insurance premiums are generally deductible under section 162(a) as ordinary and necessary expenses when paid or incurred in connection with a trade or business
The deductibility of insurance premiums depends on whether the payments were truly payments for insurance
If the captive insurance company and the business are related, the payment may resemble self-insurance, raising doubts about its deductibility
To qualify as insurance for federal income tax purposes, the arrangement must achieve risk distribution
Risk distribution is necessary for the existence of insurance
The IRS and courts have held that failure to achieve risk distribution is enough to conclude that the transactions were not insurance transactions for federal income tax purposes

verdicts.why: T.C. Memo. 2025-25 states insurance premiums are deductible under section 162(a) as ordinary and necessary expenses.
T.C. Memo. 2025-25 explicitly states deductibility depends on whether payments were truly payments for insurance.
T.C. Memo. 2025-25 states this line becomes blurred when insured and insurer are related, raising doubts about deductibility.
T.C. Memo. 2025-81 and prior cases establish risk distribution is required to qualify as insurance for tax purposes.
T.C. Memo. 2025-81 cites AMERCO holding risk distribution is necessary to the existence of insurance.
T.C. Memo. 2025-81 states failure to achieve risk distribution is enough to conclude transactions were not insurance for tax purposes.

claims: The 90-day filing deadline in I.R.C. § 6234(a) is not jurisdictional
The Tax Court has held that deadlines to file a TEFRA petition are jurisdictional
The specific 90-day deadline in I.R.C. § 6234(a) is not treated as jurisdictional
The Tax Court does not lose jurisdiction if a petition is filed a few days after the 90-day deadline

verdicts.why: 167 T.C. No. 7 holds the 90-day filing deadline in I.R.C. § 6234(a) is not jurisdictional.
167 T.C. No. 11 states Tax Court held TEFRA petition deadlines were jurisdictional in North Wall Holdings.
Claim 0 establishes the 90-day deadline in § 6234(a) is not treated as jurisdictional per 167 T.C. No. 7.
If the 90-day deadline is not jurisdictional, the court does not lose jurisdiction over late-filed petitions.

claims: A taxpayer may establish the amount of business travel expenditures by approximations based upon reliable secondary sources of information and collateral evidence when records are incomplete or documentary proof is unavailable
